question: The Nyquist-Shannon theorem provides an upper bound for the sampling period when designing a Kalman filter. Leaving apart the computational cost, are there any other reasons, e.g., noise-related issues, to set a lower bound for the sampling period? And, if so, is there an optimal value between these bounds?

sections.title: Upper Bound Constraints
sections.text: The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem establishes the primary upper limit for the sampling period in Kalman filter design. Specifically, the sampling frequency must not be less than twice the maximum frequency intended for recording [2]. In a specific application context, this principle dictates that the minimum required sampling frequency is 2.0 Hz, which corresponds to a maximum allowed sampling period of 0.5 s [1]. Consequently, the sampling rate of the recorded data strictly limits the range of frequencies that can be processed.

sections.title: Lower Bound Determinants
sections.text: Beyond computational costs, several noise-related and system-dynamic factors necessitate a lower bound for the sampling period. The sampling period is a key index that directly affects the final estimation error [4]. To maintain stability and accuracy, the sampling time should be at least two times less than the minimum system time constant [3]. Furthermore, the lower sampling period bound can be estimated using schedulability criteria. In systems involving force sensing via Kalman filters and disturbance observers, the cut-off frequency is inversely proportional to the sampling period; therefore, increasing the bandwidth is constrained by noise limits.

sections.text: Kalman filters are frequently employed to model frequency drift, such as in adaptive oscillator models for TCXO characteristics when GPS time reference signals are lost [5]. In these scenarios, components like IIRF1 are used to attenuate GPS receiver noise [5]. The effectiveness of the filter depends on its ability to handle unknown noise statistics, a problem addressed by self-tuning Kalman filters for high-maneuvering targets through system identification. A survey of Bayesian filters, including the standard Kalman filter, Extended Kalman Filter (EKF), Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF), and adaptive Sage-Husa filter, provides the context for these adaptive mechanisms. Time-domain Kalman filters offer fast convergence and good tracking properties, particularly in tracking time-varying noise conditions where LMS and RLS algorithms often struggle.

Intelligent context-aware networks in 6G leverage these capabilities to enhance service delivery [1]. sections.title: Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC)
sections.text: A key enabler for context-aware reliability is the joint and robust design of task-oriented communications, semantic communications, and integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) within a multi-task learning framework [4]. ISAC integrates sensing capabilities directly into communication access points, eliminating the need for dedicated sensor hardware. This approach supports applications such as elderly monitoring, building analytics, and V2V driver assistance. However, current research combining communication and sensing remains limited to vision and range simulations, indicating a gap in broader implementation [3].

Overall, the joint and robust design of task-oriented communications, semantic communications, and integrated sensing and communications in a multi-task learning framework emerges as the key enabler for context-aware, resource-efficient, and secure communications ultimately needed in NextG network systems.

This approach employs deep neural networks representing a dedicated encoder at the transmitter and multiple task-specific decoders at the receiver, collectively trained to handle diverse tasks including semantic information preservation, source input reconstruction, and integrated sensing and communications.

sections.title: Algorithmic Approaches and Complexity
sections.text: The fundamental problem of subgraph counting in large input graphs has a rich history, with recent work focusing on subquadratic time algorithms for bounded-degeneracy graphs [8]. While exact counting of constant-size subgraphs is polynomial-time solvable, traditional off-line methods that require storing the whole graph are often impractical for large datasets [7]. To address these limitations, various algorithmic strategies have been proposed, including a GraphBLAS approach for subgraph counting [6] and a randomized algorithm known as extensor [5]. However, without further assumptions, the best possible algorithm for this problem is likely to have a running time of $f(k) \cdot n^{\Theta(k)}$, indicating inherent computational challenges [4].

This characteristic necessitates methods that can adapt to time-varying properties rather than relying on global frequency analysis.

sections.title: Core Nonlinear Analysis Techniques
sections.text: Three common analysis methods for nonlinear signals are identified: Wavelet spectrum, Hilbert spectral analysis (HSA), and Poincare mapping [3][3][3]. Selecting the most suitable method quickly for a nonlinear signal is particularly important to improve signal processing efficiency [3]. Wavelet spectrum analysis has a good effect on concentrating on a particular band of system characteristics [3]. Poincare mapping is suited to achieve the chaotic characteristics of a system for identifying its operating status [3]. Hilbert spectral analysis (HSA) is part of the Hilbert-Huang Transform (HHT), which consists of two parts: empirical mode decomposition (EMD) and HSA [3]. In this process, the Hilbert transform is applied to each Intrinsic Mode Function (IMF) to compute instantaneous frequency and amplitude, resulting in the Hilbert-Huang spectrum [3].
